title: content/die_panel/die_panel.json
description: M7-05 — the loc keys the Die Panel (S12) renders. What is fixed here is that the panel carries a heading, a name and an effect line for each of the six face kinds, a caption for the face last rolled, and two status lines. Every value is a loc key, so a key this document names but a locale does not carry fails the build, and a locale string this document stops naming fails it as an orphan. Both face groups require all six members: the panel exists because a hidden die is a hostile die, so a face kind that had no line here would be a face the player could roll and never read about. additionalProperties is false throughout, which is what makes two absences enforced rather than merely observed. There is no member for a face's TIER and none for the source that granted it, because no client can read the composed die at all — the type that would compose one is internal to the rules and is not wired to a run; `status.facesUnavailable` is where the panel says so in words instead. And no effect line may be joined by a magnitude member, because every face's magnitude is a tunable owned by the rules and a second copy of it here could not be tuned with the first.

locKey.description: loc.<domain>.<id>.<field>, lowercase, dot-separated, snake_case segments — the same shape schema/loc.schema.json governs the locale files by.

name.description: The panel's heading and one name per face kind. All six are required, because the panel lists the vocabulary rather than the player's own die, and a vocabulary with a hole in it is the hidden die this screen exists to prevent.

effect.description: One line per face kind saying what it does. Its identity, never its magnitude — see this schema's own description.

label.description: The caption over the face the last accepted roll reported. The one thing about the player's OWN die this panel can honestly show, because it is observed rather than composed.

status.description: The line shown before any roll has been observed, and the panel's admission that the composed die is not readable. The second is a required member rather than an optional one on purpose: while the die cannot be read, a panel that quietly showed six generic faces would be asserting a die the player may not have.
